title: Major Depression: Diagnose the Episode, Assess Safety Every Time
bottomLine: Major depressive disorder requires a depressive syndrome with clinically meaningful impairment after bipolar, substance, medication and medical causes are considered. Suicide assessment is part of every clinically significant depressive presentation, not a separate optional screen.
recognize: Low mood or loss of interest with sleep, appetite, energy, cognition, guilt or psychomotor change can define the syndrome.
differentiate: Past mania or hypomania changes the diagnosis and antidepressant strategy; bereavement can coexist with major depression.
assessment: Assess symptom duration and function, suicide/self-harm, psychosis, past mania, substances, trauma, pregnancy, medications and medical mimics.
workup: Use validated symptom scales to support measurement, not replace interview; labs are targeted to plausible medical causes.
management: Use psychotherapy, antidepressant medication or combination based on severity and preference; severe psychotic, catatonic or high-risk depression needs urgent psychiatry and may require ECT or other specialty treatment.
medicationSafety: Monitor activation, emerging mania, adverse effects and early suicide-risk changes after treatment starts; do not stop antidepressants abruptly without a taper plan when discontinuation symptoms are likely.
redFlags: Active suicidal intent or inability to maintain safety
counselling: Set expectations that response is monitored over weeks and treatment is adjusted using symptoms, function and tolerability.
followUp: Use early follow-up after initiation or dose changes, with closer review for high-risk patients.
examTrap: Starting an antidepressant for depression without ever asking about prior mania or hypomania.
oneLinePearl: Before calling depression unipolar, ask whether the patient has ever been too high.

title: Bipolar Disorder: Antidepressant Monotherapy Can Destabilize
bottomLine: Bipolar disorder is defined by mania or hypomania history, not by mood swings alone. Acute mania with dangerous behaviour, psychosis or inability to care for self may require hospitalization; antidepressant monotherapy is generally inappropriate for bipolar I depression.
recognize: Mania includes persistently elevated or irritable mood with increased energy plus decreased sleep need, pressured speech, racing thoughts, grandiosity, impulsivity or increased goal-directed activity.
differentiate: Substance-induced activation, ADHD, personality patterns and unipolar depression can mimic parts of bipolar illness.
assessment: Ask lifetime mood episodes, sleep need, impairment, psychosis, spending/sexual/risk behaviour, substances, family history, pregnancy and suicide risk.
workup: Use thyroid, toxicology and other medical testing when indicated; diagnosis remains clinical.
management: Use CANMAT/ISBD evidence-based mood stabilizers or atypical antipsychotics based on episode type; urgent psychiatry for severe mania, mixed states or psychosis.
medicationSafety: Lithium requires renal, thyroid, level and interaction monitoring and carries pregnancy considerations; valproate has major teratogenic risk and should be avoided in pregnancy when possible.
counselling: Teach sleep regularity, relapse signs and medication interaction monitoring.
followUp: Monitor mood polarity, adherence, metabolic effects and organ-specific medication labs.
examTrap: Prescribing SSRI monotherapy to a patient with a past unequivocal manic episode.
oneLinePearl: A history of mania changes the whole antidepressant conversation.
sourceBasis: CANMAT and ISBD Bipolar Disorder guideline

title: Anxiety and Panic: Rule Out the Mimic, Then Treat the Pattern
bottomLine: Anxiety disorders are diagnosed from persistent fear or worry patterns and impairment after urgent medical mimics are considered. A first episode of palpitations, dyspnea or chest pain should not be labelled panic before cardiopulmonary and substance causes are assessed.
recognize: Panic attacks peak rapidly with intense autonomic symptoms; generalized anxiety is persistent excessive worry across domains.
differentiate: Arrhythmia, ACS, PE, hyperthyroidism, asthma, stimulant/caffeine use and withdrawal can mimic panic.
assessment: Assess onset, triggers, avoidance, function, substances, sleep, depression/suicide risk and trauma.
workup: Use targeted ECG, thyroid or other testing when clinical features suggest a medical cause, not routine broad panels for established recurrent panic.
management: CBT and SSRIs/SNRIs are core long-term treatments; exposure-based strategies are important for panic and phobic avoidance.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can cause dependence, falls and dangerous interaction with opioids or alcohol and are not preferred long-term monotherapy.
counselling: Explain that panic symptoms are physiologically real and treatable without implying that every episode is medically dangerous.
followUp: Track avoidance and function, not just symptom frequency.
examTrap: Diagnosing panic disorder from a single first episode of chest pain and tachycardia without a basic medical assessment.
oneLinePearl: Panic is a pattern diagnosis; the first attack still deserves a differential.

title: PTSD: Trauma-Informed Assessment Without Forced Disclosure
bottomLine: PTSD includes trauma-related intrusion, avoidance, negative mood or cognition and hyperarousal with impairment. Trauma-informed care prioritizes safety, choice and control; the clinician does not need to force a detailed trauma narrative to validate symptoms or start care.
recognize: Nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance and emotional numbing are common.
differentiate: Acute stress disorder is time-limited soon after trauma; depression, panic and substance use often coexist.
assessment: Ask permission before trauma questions; assess current safety, suicide risk, sleep, substance use, dissociation and intimate-partner violence.
workup: Use validated PTSD screening tools to support assessment; no laboratory test diagnoses PTSD.
management: Trauma-focused psychotherapies are first-line; medications can target PTSD or comorbid symptoms when indicated.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine long-term benzodiazepines for PTSD because they can impair recovery and create dependence risk.
counselling: Offer grounding and choice, and explain that disclosure depth is patient-controlled.
followUp: Coordinate psychotherapy access and reassess safety and function.
examTrap: Insisting that a patient recount a traumatic event in detail during the first visit before offering care.
oneLinePearl: Trauma-informed care gives control back; it does not demand a story as proof.

title: First-Episode Psychosis: Safety, Cause, Early Treatment
bottomLine: New hallucinations, delusions or disorganization require assessment for immediate safety and for substance, medication, delirium, neurologic and metabolic causes. Early psychosis treatment improves outcomes, but new psychosis in an older adult is a medical syndrome until proven otherwise.
recognize: Functional decline, social withdrawal and thought disorder may precede overt psychosis in young people.
differentiate: Delirium has impaired attention and fluctuating course; mania can include psychosis; stimulants/cannabis and steroids can precipitate psychotic symptoms.
assessment: Assess violence/suicide risk, command hallucinations, ability to care for self, substances, medications, cognition/attention, neurologic symptoms and collateral history.
workup: Use targeted CBC/chemistry/thyroid/pregnancy/toxicology or neuroimaging when the clinical pattern warrants; avoid unselective panels.
management: Urgently refer unsafe, severely disorganized or medically unstable patients; use early psychosis services and antipsychotic treatment with psychosocial support when a primary psychotic disorder is established.
medicationSafety: Antipsychotics require metabolic and movement-disorder monitoring; QT risk and drug interactions matter.
counselling: Engage family or chosen supports with consent and use non-confrontational communication about fixed beliefs.
followUp: Monitor diagnosis over time because initial psychosis labels can evolve.
examTrap: Calling a new hallucination in an 82-year-old schizophrenia before checking for delirium and medication toxicity.
oneLinePearl: First psychosis in later life is medical until proven otherwise.

title: OCD: Obsessions Are Not the Same as Psychosis
bottomLine: OCD causes intrusive unwanted obsessions and repetitive compulsions or mental rituals that reduce distress temporarily. Exposure and response prevention is a core treatment, often combined with an SSRI; insight can vary without making obsessions delusions.
recognize: Contamination, harm, symmetry, sexual or religious intrusive thoughts can occur and are often ego-dystonic.
differentiate: Psychosis involves impaired reality testing; generalized anxiety lacks ritualized neutralizing compulsions; OCPD is a personality pattern rather than intrusive obsession-compulsion cycles.
assessment: Ask time consumed, avoidance, family accommodation, suicidality/depression, tic disorder and perinatal onset.
workup: No routine medical testing is needed for a typical presentation.
management: Use CBT with exposure and response prevention and guideline-supported pharmacotherapy; severe refractory illness warrants specialty care.
medicationSafety: Effective SSRI doses for OCD may be higher than for depression and require careful titration; avoid abrupt discontinuation.
redFlags: Inability to eat/drink due to rituals
counselling: Normalize intrusive thoughts and explain that having a thought does not imply intent.
followUp: Track time spent in rituals and functional recovery.
examTrap: Treating ego-dystonic intrusive harm thoughts as proof that the patient intends to harm someone.
oneLinePearl: OCD thoughts are unwanted signals, not intentions.

title: Insomnia: CBT-I Before Chronic Sedatives
bottomLine: Chronic insomnia is persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep with daytime impairment despite adequate opportunity. CBT-I is first-line; chronic hypnotic prescribing should not replace evaluation of sleep apnea, restless legs, mood, substances and circadian patterns.
recognize: Conditioned arousal and extended time in bed can perpetuate insomnia.
differentiate: OSA causes sleep fragmentation and sleepiness; mania causes decreased need for sleep rather than distress about inability to sleep.
assessment: Use sleep schedule, naps, caffeine/alcohol/cannabis, medications, snoring/apneas, leg symptoms, mood and work schedule.
workup: Sleep study is for suspected sleep-disordered breathing or other specific disorders, not routine insomnia.
management: Use CBT-I components including stimulus control and sleep consolidation; medication is adjunctive and individualized.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs increase falls, cognitive impairment and dependence risk, especially in older adults.
counselling: Explain that spending more time awake in bed can worsen insomnia.
followUp: Track sleep efficiency and daytime function.
examTrap: Starting nightly benzodiazepine in an older adult before asking about sleep apnea and falls.
oneLinePearl: Chronic insomnia is treated with sleep behaviour, not just sedation.

title: ADHD Across the Lifespan: Impairment in More Than One Setting
bottomLine: ADHD is a persistent neurodevelopmental pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity causing impairment across settings, with symptoms beginning in childhood. A questionnaire alone does not diagnose it.
recognize: School/work disorganization, forgetfulness, impulsivity and task-completion difficulty are common.
differentiate: Sleep deprivation, anxiety, depression, trauma, substance use, learning disorders and bipolar disorder can mimic or coexist with ADHD.
assessment: Obtain developmental history and collateral information when possible, assess multiple settings, comorbidities, substance use, sleep and cardiovascular history.
workup: No routine neuroimaging or laboratory panel diagnoses ADHD; testing is targeted to mimics or learning needs.
management: Use behavioural/environmental supports and evidence-based stimulant or non-stimulant medication according to age, severity and preference.
medicationSafety: Monitor BP, HR, growth in children, appetite, sleep and misuse/diversion risk; screen for bipolar and substance concerns.
counselling: Discuss school/work accommodations and safe medication storage.
followUp: Track functional goals, not just symptom scores.
examTrap: Diagnosing adult ADHD solely from current concentration problems during a depressive episode with no childhood history.
oneLinePearl: ADHD is lifelong neurodevelopmental impairment, not a new adult concentration symptom.

title: Eating Disorders: Medical Instability Can Hide Behind Appearance
bottomLine: Eating disorders occur at any body size. Bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte disturbance, syncope, acute food refusal, purging and suicidality determine medical urgency—not appearance or BMI alone.
recognize: Restriction, bingeing, compensatory behaviours, body-image disturbance and compulsive exercise can occur in multiple diagnoses.
differentiate: GI disease, diabetes, thyroid disease and depression can cause weight or appetite change but do not explain eating-disorder cognitions and behaviours.
assessment: Ask privately about restriction, bingeing, vomiting/laxatives, exercise, menses, syncope, substance use, suicide and weight history; obtain orthostatic vitals and cardiac exam.
workup: Use electrolytes, glucose, magnesium/phosphate, CBC, liver/renal tests and ECG according to severity; assess pregnancy when relevant.
management: Medically unstable patients need urgent specialized assessment; stable patients require evidence-based psychotherapy/nutrition and coordinated primary care.
medicationSafety: Bupropion is contraindicated in bulimia/anorexia because seizure risk is increased; refeeding can cause dangerous electrolyte shifts.
counselling: Avoid praise or moral judgment about weight; focus on medical safety and recovery.
followUp: Track vitals, behaviours, labs and psychosocial recovery through an eating-disorder team.
examTrap: Reassuring a normal-BMI patient with daily purging because they do not look underweight.
oneLinePearl: Eating-disorder severity is behavioural and physiologic, not visible.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society adolescent eating-disorder resources

title: Perinatal Mental Health: Screen Depression, Anxiety, Bipolarity, and Psychosis
bottomLine: Pregnancy and postpartum periods can precipitate depression, anxiety, OCD, bipolar episodes and psychosis. Treatment decisions balance maternal illness risk with fetal or infant exposure; untreated severe illness is not the safe default.
recognize: Postpartum psychosis often emerges rapidly with insomnia, mania, confusion, delusions or hallucinations and is an emergency.
differentiate: Transient postpartum blues are mild and brief; persistent impairment, suicidality or psychosis is not normal adjustment.
assessment: Assess depression/anxiety/OCD symptoms, bipolar history, psychosis, sleep, suicide and infant-harm thoughts with intent versus ego-dystonic obsessions, supports and substance use.
workup: Use validated perinatal screens and medical testing when thyroid, anemia or other contributors are plausible.
management: Use CANMAT 2024 perinatal guidance for psychotherapy and medication decisions; hospitalize postpartum psychosis or unsafe severe illness.
medicationSafety: Avoid abrupt discontinuation of effective psychiatric medication solely because pregnancy occurs; valproate has major reproductive risk and requires specialist planning.
redFlags: Severe inability to sleep or care for self/infant
counselling: Discuss risks of both treatment and untreated illness using shared decision-making.
followUp: Arrange early postpartum follow-up for high-risk patients and coordinated psychiatry-obstetric care.
examTrap: Automatically stopping an effective antidepressant as soon as pregnancy is confirmed without assessing relapse risk.
oneLinePearl: Perinatal safety includes the risk of untreated illness, not just medication exposure.
sourceBasis: CANMAT 2024 Perinatal Mood, Anxiety, and Related Disorders guideline

title: Delirium: Acute Brain Failure Until the Cause Is Found
bottomLine: Acute fluctuating inattention and cognitive change is delirium, not dementia progression, until a precipitating medical cause is found. Treat causes and use non-pharmacologic safety measures; antipsychotics do not cure delirium.
recognize: Inattention, fluctuating alertness and disorganized thinking can be hyperactive or hypoactive.
differentiate: Dementia is chronic and progressive; depression can mimic cognitive impairment but does not typically produce fluctuating inattention.
assessment: Check oxygenation, glucose, infection, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, medications, withdrawal and environment; obtain collateral baseline cognition.
workup: Use targeted labs, urinalysis only when urinary infection is clinically plausible, imaging when focal/trauma features exist, and avoid indiscriminate testing.
management: Correct causes, orient/reassure, mobilize, restore hearing/vision and sleep, minimize lines/restraints and involve family; reserve medication for severe dangerous agitation when non-drug measures fail.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can worsen most delirium except alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal; anticholinergics and sedatives are common precipitants.
counselling: Explain that delirium is an acute medical syndrome and recovery may lag after the trigger is treated.
followUp: Reassess cognition after recovery because delirium can unmask underlying cognitive disease.
examTrap: Ordering antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria solely because a confused older adult has a positive urine culture.
oneLinePearl: Delirium is acute brain failure: find the trigger, do not sedate the label.

title: Suicide Risk: Ask Directly and Build a Real Safety Plan
bottomLine: Suicide risk assessment is direct, collaborative and action-oriented. Determine current thoughts, intent, plan, access to lethal means, recent behaviour, substance use, protective factors and ability to maintain safety; a no-harm contract is not a substitute for a safety plan or appropriate level of care.
recognize: Recent attempt, active intent, escalating planning, intoxication, psychosis, agitation and access to lethal means increase immediate risk.
differentiate: Passive death wishes and active suicidal intent are different but both deserve assessment; protective factors do not cancel serious acute risk.
assessment: Ask directly about ideation, intent, plan, preparation, past attempts, lethal means, substances, psychosis, supports and reasons for living.
workup: Medical testing is guided by overdose, intoxication, injury or medical contributors, not routine psychiatric panels.
management: Use emergency psychiatric care and continuous safety measures when imminent risk cannot be managed outpatient; for appropriate outpatient care, create a collaborative written safety plan and reduce lethal-means access.
medicationSafety: Limit quantities of highly lethal medications when acute risk is significant and coordinate medication access with supports when consent and safety allow.
redFlags: Inability to collaborate on immediate safety
counselling: Asking about suicide does not create suicidal thoughts; use direct nonjudgmental language.
followUp: Arrange rapid follow-up and proactive contact after crisis or discharge.
examTrap: Relying on a signed 'no-suicide contract' as evidence that discharge is safe.
oneLinePearl: Safety planning is an intervention; a promise not to self-harm is not.
